title: Laughter: What's so funny about that?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how laughter works, drawing on a HowStuffWorks article by Marshall Brain. They cover the difference between humor and laughter, the physical cascade of laughing (facial muscles, breathing, epiglottis, tear ducts), universal "ha ha"/"ho ho" sounds, signature laughs, contagion, the punctuation effect, the church giggles, social bonding and dominance theories, laughing gas and solitary laughter, gelotology, the brain's neural circuit for humor, incongruity and superiority theories, Alistair Cooke's humor formula, relief theory, what makes things unfunny (age and attachment to the subject), cultural differences in humor, and the health benefits of laughter (immune response, workout, Norman Cousins, UCLA cold-water pain study). The episode ends with a listener mail bear story from Chris F. in Vancouver and Kiva and video podcast promos.

segments.title: Opening banter and Louis C.K. and Anthony Jeselnick clips
segments.summary: The hosts open with jokes about airport cinnamon buns, a Louis C.K. bit, and an Anthony Jeselnick joke, then set up the episode on how laughter works based on a HowStuffWorks article.

segments.title: Humor versus laughter and the physical laugh response
segments.summary: Laughter is defined as the physiological response to humor. The hosts describe facial muscles contracting (zygomatic major), the epiglottis closing the larynx, breathlessness, tear ducts, and snorting.

segments.title: Universal laugh sounds and signature laughs
segments.summary: People worldwide produce similar 'ha ha' or 'ho ho' sounds at about the same rate, and each person has a signature laugh. The hosts also discuss laughter being contagious.

segments.title: Punctuation effect and church giggles
segments.summary: Laughter tends to occur at the end of sentences or phrases, the punctuation effect, and stifling laughter makes situations funnier, as with church giggles. GoodFellas is cited as an example.

segments.title: Origins of laughter: relief, social bonding, dominance
segments.summary: Theories of why laughter evolved include relief after danger (Tuck and the saber-tooth tigers), social bonding requiring trust, and asserting dominance. Studies found people are far more likely to laugh in social settings than alone.

segments.title: Laughing gas and solitary laughter
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Willibald Roth's finding that nitrous oxide is less effective when people are alone, and talk about dental experiences with laughing gas. They also note gelotology as the physiological study of laughter.

segments.title: Brain circuitry of humor
segments.summary: Humor involves all parts of the brain according to EEG studies. A wave moves through the cortex, with the left hemisphere analyzing words, the frontal lobe handling emotion, the right hemisphere making sense of the joke, the occipital lobe visualizing, and motor areas producing physical responses.

segments.title: Incongruity, superiority, and the humor formula
segments.summary: Incongruity theory says humor comes from a surprising mismatch with expectations. Superiority theory explains laughing at others' misfortune. Alistair Cooke's formula ties humor to misinformation and believability. Comedy is tragedy plus time is also mentioned.

segments.title: Relief theory, Mexican standoffs, and what bends or breaks
segments.summary: Relief theory is illustrated by a baby scared of his mom blowing his nose and by laughter defusing a standoff. Alan Alda's line from Crimes and Misdemeanors, 'if it bends it's funny, if it breaks it's not,' is discussed.

segments.title: Why things aren't funny: age, attachment, intelligence, culture
segments.summary: Robert Provine's research suggests that age and attachment to the subject or victim determine whether something is funny. Culture also shapes humor, with Borat and British humor cited.

segments.title: Health benefits of laughter
segments.summary: Laughter reduces stress hormones and boosts immune markers, and is compared to exercise. Norman Cousins found Marx Brothers films eased his pain. A UCLA study had children hold hands in cold water and lasted longer when watching funny videos.

segments.title: Sign-off, listener mail, and promos
segments.summary: Chuck reads a listener mail bear story from Chris F. in Vancouver about a bear cub and mother raiding his garbage. The hosts close with Kiva and video podcast promos.
